rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing God’s mercy toward people despite their ingratitude, the passage turns to His favor in prescribing religious duties.
rows.anchor: إعلم أنه تعالى لما قدم ذكر نعمه وبين أنه رؤوف رحيم بعباده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse lacks an initial conjunction because this statement is not attached to what preceded it.
rows.anchor: إنما حذف الواو في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes a manسك as a festival at which the community slaughters an animal.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس عيد ( ا ) يذبحون فيه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the term as a sacrificial offering and says it is specifically used for slaughter.
rows.anchor: ولفظ المنسك مختص بالذبائح عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قول ثالث
rows.claim: A third view understands the term as a familiar place or time appointed for acts of worship.
rows.anchor: مألفا يألفونه إما مكانا معينا أو زمانا معينا لأداء الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers the view attributed to Ibn Abbas through ʿAṭāʾ and chosen by al-Qaffāl: manسك means a religious law or path, since worship is not limited to sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس في رواية عطاء واختيار القفال وهو الأقرب لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He derives manسك from worship; since the name can cover every act of worship, restricting it to sacrifice lacks justification.
rows.anchor: إذا وقع الإسم على كل عبادة فلا وجه للتخصيص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against restricting manسك to slaughter by customary usage, Rāzī notes that all the rites of pilgrimage are called manāsik, as in the Prophet’s instruction to learn them from him.
rows.anchor: أن سائر ما يفعل في الحج يوصف بأنه مناسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “they practice it” fits worship better than a specific place or time, answering the proposed place-and-time interpretation.
rows.anchor: أليق بالعبادة منه بالوقت والمكان

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some restrict the communities meant to Jews and Christians who adhered to a revealed law in Muhammad’s lifetime.
rows.anchor: زعم قوم أن المراد من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī allows the verse to include worshippers from every nation, whether their religious traces still remain or not; “they practice it” describes the communities without requiring present worship.
rows.anchor: ولا يمتنع أن يريد كل من تعبد من الأمم سواء بقيت آثارهم أو لم تبق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading of the phrase is understood as commanding Muhammad to remain steadfast in his religion so opponents cannot entice him away.
rows.anchor: أي أثبت في دينك ثباتا لا يطمعون أن يخدعوك

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj reads the prohibition as addressed to the opponents: they must not contend with Muhammad, like the idiom “do not fight him.”
rows.anchor: قول الزجاج : أنه نهى لهم عن منازعتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation requires the communities to follow Muhammad and abandon opposition, since his law has become established and supersedes earlier laws; surviving adherents must convert.
rows.anchor: أن المراد أن عليهم اتباعك وترك مخالفتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad is to call every nation, without excluding any, to his law because all are included among those he addresses.
rows.anchor: أي لا تخص بالدعاء أمة دون أمة فكلهم أمتك فادعهم إلى شريعتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance could mean the religion itself or its proofs; Rāzī prefers the proofs, a clear path by which the religion is demonstrated.
rows.anchor: والهدى يحتمل نفس الدين ويحتمل أدلة الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If opponents leave examination of the proofs for disputation and appeals to custom, Muhammad has made his case; warning them that God knows their deeds is then appropriate.
rows.anchor: فإن عدلوا عن النظر في هذه الأدلة إلى طريقة المراء والتمسك بالعادة فقد بينت وأظهرت ما يلزمك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning points to the final judgment, when people will recognize truth and falsehood and God will decide their disputes, rewarding acceptance and punishing rejection.
rows.anchor: ليس بعد إيضاح الأدلة إلا هذا الجنس الذي يجري مجرى الوعيد والتحذير من حكم يوم القيامة

none: Only a quotation of neighboring verses; no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding command to worship, Rāzī turns to evidence for God’s existence, majesty, and oneness, since worship requires knowing the Creator.
rows.anchor: اعلم أنه سبحانه لما أمر بالعبادات في الآية المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human development is presented as one of several proofs, proceeding through nine stages of creation.
rows.anchor: الاستدلال يتقلب الإنسان في أدوار الخلقة وأكوان الفطرة وهي تسعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sullāla means the extracted essence, sifted out from what is turbid.
rows.anchor: والسلالة الخلاصة لأنها تسل من بين الكدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form faʿāla indicates a small quantity, as do qalāma and qumāma.
rows.anchor: فعالة وهو بناء يدل على القلة كالقلامة والقمامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة وقتادة ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, and Muqātil take “the human” as Adam, extracted from clay, while his descendants were made from lowly fluid.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وعكرمة وقتادة ومقاتل

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others take “the human” as Adam’s child and “clay” as Adam; clay particles in Adam’s body gathered in the semen vessels and became semen.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : الإنسان ههنا ولد آدم والطين ههنا اسم آدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī also explains the wording through human nutrition: semen derives from the residue of the fourth digestion, food ultimately derives from plants, and plants from earth and water; he says this fits the wording without forced interpretation.
rows.anchor: فالإنسان بالحقيقة يكون متولدا من سلالة من طين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interpretation connecting human beings to clay and semen corresponds to the account that human creation began from clay and descendants from a fluid extract.
rows.anchor: وبدأ خلق الإنسان من طين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God first created human substance from clay, then made it semen in the fathers’ loins and conveyed it through intercourse into the woman’s womb.
rows.anchor: ومعنى جعل الإنسان نطفة أنه خلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarār denotes the place where something settles; the womb is called by the verbal noun for its settled location and is described as secure.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالقرار موضع القرار وهو المستقر فسماه بالمصدر ثم وصف الرحم بالمكانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī gives two explanations of the womb’s being makīn: the description may transfer from what is settled there, or refer to the womb’s own secure, protected position.
rows.anchor: كقولك طريق سائر أو لمكانتها في نفسها لأنها تمكنت من حيث هي وأحرزت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third stage changes semen from its former qualities into the qualities of an ʿalaqa, a clotted mass of blood.
rows.anchor: أي حولنا النطفة عن صفاتها إلى صفات العلقة وهي الدم الجامد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A muḍgha is a piece of flesh about the size of a morsel one could chew, like a gharfa is a quantity one could scoop.
rows.anchor: أي جعلنا ذلك الدم الجامد مضغة أي قطعة لحم كأنها مقدار ما يمضغ كالغرفة وهي مقدار ما يغترف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling this transformation “creation” means God removes some of the mass’s accidents, creates other accidents, and adds further parts.
rows.anchor: وسمى التحويل خلقا لأنه سبحانه يفني بعض أعراضها ويخلق أعراضا غيرها

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the word as singular ʿaẓm, intended collectively, as in the expression “rank upon rank.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر عظما والمراد منه الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording pictures flesh as clothing because it covers the bones.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن اللحم يستر العظم فجعله كالكسوة لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seventh stage is a radically distinct creation: formerly inert and mute, the human becomes living, articulate, hearing, and seeing, with wonders of wisdom in every part.
rows.anchor: أي خلقا مباينا للخلق الأول مباينة

rows.speaker: العوفي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-ʿAwfī reports Ibn Abbas’s view that the phrase covers God’s development of a person after birth through childhood, youth, understanding, and intellect until death.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما قال : هو تصريف الله إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The postnatal-life interpretation is supported by the next verse’s statement that people will later die; Rāzī also says this meaning is reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وهذا المعنى مروي أيضا عن ابن عباس وابن عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “created anew” suits the creation of the spirit within the human and the completion of his formation.
rows.anchor: لأنه جعل إنشاء الروح فيه ، وإتمام خلقه إنشاء له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī treats the description of the human as a composite of these created traits as evidence against al-Naẓẓām’s claim that the human is the spirit rather than the body.
rows.anchor: قالوا في الآية دلالة على بطلان قول النظام في أن الإنسان هو الروح لا البدن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also says the verse refutes philosophers who describe the human as indivisible and not a body.
rows.anchor: وفيها دلالة أيضا على بطلان قول الفلاسفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabāraka can mean that God is exalted, since blessing involves extension or increase and what increases rises above what it exceeds.
rows.anchor: فإن البركة يرجع معناها إلى الامتداد والزيادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, all blessings and good things come from God, who therefore deserves praise and reverence.
rows.anchor: والبركات والخيرات كلها من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قول
rows.claim: Another etymology derives the expression from burūk, stability: God is enduring and everlasting, and all blessings come from Him.
rows.anchor: وقيل أصله من البروك وهو الثبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥsan al-khāliqīn means “best of estimators”; the understood qualifier “in estimation” is omitted because the word “creators” indicates it.
rows.anchor: أي أحسن المقدرين تقديرا فترك ذكر المميز لدلالة الخالقين عليه

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites argue that calling God the best creator presupposes other creators; humans create their acts by deliberate estimation, just as humans can be described as wise judges or merciful.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة لولا أن الله تعالى قد يكون خالقا لفعله إذا قدره لما جاز القول بأنه أحسن الخالقين

rows.speaker: الكعبي
rows.claim: Al-Kaʿbī says a human may be called a creator only with a qualification, just as someone may be “master of a house” but not simply “Lord.”
rows.anchor: قال الكعبي هذه الآية ، وإن دلت على أن العبد خالق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects explaining the plural as referring only to Jesus: the plural is broader, and if Jesus counts as a creator, image-makers would too.
rows.anchor: الذين هم جمع فحمله على عيسى خاصة لا يصح

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Rāzī’s fellow theologians answer that God is creator of everything (39:62), so “best creators” means best in people’s belief, as “easier for Him” is likewise contextual (30:27).
rows.anchor: وأجاب أصحابنا بأن هذه الآية معارضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another answer takes creator to mean estimator; but estimation as conjecture or calculation is impossible for God, making the verse among the ambiguous texts.
rows.anchor: هو أن الخالق هو المقدر لأن الخلق هو التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if a human is a creator in the sense of estimating, that does not establish that a human originates things.
rows.anchor: لكن لم قلت بأنه خالق بمعنى كونه موجدا

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites infer that if everything God creates is good and wise, He cannot create unbelief or sin; therefore humans must originate those acts.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة الآية تدل على أن كل ما خلقه حسن وحكمة وصواب وإلا لما جاز وصفه بأنه أحسن الخالقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that “good” can mean exact construction and composition; even if it means goodness and wisdom, all acts are good from God, who is bound by no higher command or prohibition.
rows.anchor: من الناس من حمل الحسن على الإحكام والاتقان في التركيب والتأليف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, in al-Kalbī’s report, says ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ was dictating these verses; when he heard “a different creation,” he exclaimed “Blessed is God, best of creators,” and Muhammad told him to write it as revealed.
rows.anchor: روى الكلبي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أن عبدالله بن سعد بن أبي سرح كان يكتب هذه الآيات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the same report, ʿAbd Allāh doubted Muhammad’s claim, fled to Mecca, and is said either to have died an unbeliever or to have converted at the conquest; Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: فهرب إلى مكة فقيل إنه مات على الكفر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reports Ibn Abbas’s account that ʿUmar uttered the phrase when the verse was revealed and Muhammad told him it had been revealed that way.
rows.anchor: وروى سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس قال لما نزلت هذه الآية قال عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar said God had agreed with him on four occasions: prayer behind the Station, the veil, his admonition to the Prophet’s wives (followed by 66:5), and this phrase.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر يقول : وافقني ربي في أربع

rows.speaker: العارفون
rows.claim: The gnostics say the episode brought ʿUmar good fortune and ʿAbd Allāh misery, illustrating that revelation guides some and misleads others (2:26).
rows.anchor: قال العارفون هذه الواقعة كانت سبب السعادة لعمر

rows.speaker: عبدالله بن سعد بن أبي سرح
rows.claim: The account has ʿAbd Allāh object that a human had spoken words resembling the Qur’an, which seemed to undermine its inimitability.
rows.anchor: قد تكلم البشر ابتداء بمثل نظم القرآن ، وذلك يقدح في كونه معجزا كما ظنه عبدالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that this is possible if the utterance remained at a level where the Qur’an’s miraculous quality was not evident, removing ʿAbd Allāh’s objection.
rows.anchor: هذا غير مستبعد إذا كان قدره القدر الذي لا يظهر فيه الإعجاز فسقطت شبهة عبدالله

none: Only a heading and quotation of verses 24:27-29; no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī connects the rule to the preceding slander rulings: seclusion gave people an opening for accusations, so permission and greeting are required to prevent suspicion and harm.
rows.anchor: لأن أهل الإفك إنما وجدوا السبيل إلى بهتانهم من حيث اتفقت الخلوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first question notes that istiʾnās ordinarily means sociability through companionship, apparently something that would follow entering and greeting; the Qur’an also uses it for lingering to converse.
rows.anchor: الاستئناس عبارة عن الأنس الحاصل من جهة المجالسة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr are reported to interpret the wording as “until you seek permission”; this account alleges the scribe erred.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ، إنما هو حتى تستأذنوا فأخطأ الكاتب

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading is given as “until you seek permission for yourselves.”
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة أبي : حتى تستأذنوا لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Greeting is better than the pre-Islamic greeting and than damūr, entry without permission; damūr is linked to destruction because its perpetrator has committed a grave offense.
rows.anchor: وهو الدخول بغير إذن واشتقاقه من الدمار

rows.speaker: الحديث
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says that the person whose eye precedes his request for permission has committed damūr, a serious breach.
rows.anchor: من سبقت عينه استئذانه فقد دمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects the claim that Ibn Abbas meant a scribal error: it would impugn the multiply transmitted Qur’an and privilege a non-mass-transmitted reading, opening doubt about the whole text.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا القول من ابن عباس فيه نظر لأنه يقتضي الطعن في القرآن الذي نقل بالتواتر

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī proposes fronting and delaying: the intended order is to greet the household and then seek familiarity.
rows.anchor: الحسن البصري أنه قال إن في الكلام تقديما وتأخيرا

rows.speaker: عبدالله
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh puts greeting before asking permission.
rows.anchor: قراءة عبدالله : حتى تسلموا على أهلها وتستأذنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī calls the reordered construction weak because it departs from the apparent wording.
rows.anchor: وهذا أيضا ضعيف لأنه خلاف الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the apparent wording, one explanation is that permission and greeting reassure the household, whereas unpermitted entry unsettles and burdens them.
rows.anchor: حتى تستأنسوا بالإذن وذلك لأنهم إذا استأذنوا وسلموا أنس أهل البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred explanation takes istiʾnās as seeking information or finding out whether entry is wanted, from ānasa in the sense of seeing something manifest.
rows.anchor: تفسير الاستئناس بالاستعلام والاستكشاف استفعال من آنس الشيء إذا أبصره ظاهرا مكشوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites “استأنس هل ترى أحدا” and “استأنست فلم أر أحدا” as idioms meaning to ascertain or investigate whether anyone is present.
rows.anchor: واستأنست فلم أر أحدا أي تعرفت واستعلمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When asked why greeting does not come first as in the Prophet’s formula “Peace be upon you; may I enter?”, Rāzī answers that a visitor may not know whether anyone is home; ask first, then greet face to face after permission.
rows.anchor: قلنا المستأذن ربما لا يعلم أن أحدا في المنزل فلا معنى لسلامه والحالة هذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation derives istiʾnās from ins: first establish whether a person is there, which necessarily precedes greeting.
rows.anchor: من الإنس وهو أن يتعرف هل ثم إنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth answer says that even if familiarity follows greeting, the coordinating wāw does not require chronological order, so the order of mention need not dictate the order of action.
rows.anchor: ولكن الواو لا توجب الترتيب

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying permission is sought three times: the first and second requests have the stated purposes, and at the third the household may admit or refuse.
rows.anchor: روى أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( الاستئذان )

rows.speaker: جندب
rows.claim: Jundub says he heard the Prophet instruct that a person who asks permission three times without being admitted should leave.
rows.anchor: عن جندب قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول : ( إذا استأذن أحدكم ثلاثا

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī recounts witnessing for Abū Mūsā: after Abū Mūsā left when ʿUmar failed to answer three requests, ʿUmar demanded proof of the Prophetic rule and Abū Saʿīd testified.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي سعيد الخدري قال : ( كنت جالسا في مجلس من مجالس الأنصار

rows.speaker: بعض الأخبار
rows.claim: Another account says ʿUmar told Abū Mūsā that he did not suspect him but feared people might attribute statements falsely to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الأخبار أن عمر قال لأبي موسى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains the three requests as letting occupants hear, giving them time to prepare, and allowing them to admit or refuse.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة الاستئذان ثلاثة : الأولى يسمع الحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī treats three spaced requests as proper etiquette: the first may meet occupants at work, the second may encounter an impediment, and silence at the third signals a reason or reluctance, so the visitor should leave.
rows.anchor: وفي المرة الثانية ربما كان هناك ما يمنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the three requests should not be consecutive; time should separate each one from the next.
rows.anchor: يجب في الاستئذان ثلاثا ، أن لا يكون متصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forceful knocking and shouting to the homeowner are forbidden because they cause distress and alarm; the Banū Asad incident and 49:4 warn against this conduct.
rows.anchor: فذاك حرام لأنه يتضمن الإيذاء والإيحاش

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: A report says Abū Saʿīd sought permission while facing the door; the Prophet told him not to ask permission while standing directly before it.
rows.anchor: روي أن أبا سعيد استأذن على الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو مستقبل الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says the Prophet approached a household’s door from its right or left corner, greeted them, and did not face the door directly because houses then had no curtains.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام كان إذا أتى باب قوم لم يستقبل الباب من تلقاء وجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “until” might seem to permit entry after asking without receiving consent, Rāzī says the endpoint is actual reassurance, which arises only after permission is granted.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى جعل الغاية الاستئناس لا الاستئذان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose of permission is to prevent upsetting another by entering without consent; requesting permission alone cannot achieve that purpose.
rows.anchor: أن الحكمة في الاستئذان أن لا يدخل الإنسان على غيره بغير إذنه فإن ذلك مما يسوءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 28 explicitly forbids entry when no one is present until permission is given, showing that consent is also required by the first verse.
rows.anchor: فإن لم تجدوا فيها أحدا فلا تدخلوها حتى يؤذن لكم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that a man’s messenger to another man counts as the man’s permission.
rows.anchor: روى أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ( رسول الرجل

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A second report from Abū Hurayra says a person invited to come with the messenger has permission and need not seek it again.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه عن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام قال : ( إذا دعي أحدكم فجاء مع الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports show that permission is implicit in “until you seek familiarity” and that arriving with an invitation-bearing messenger requires no second request.
rows.anchor: وهذا الخبر يدل على معنيين أحدهما : أن الإذن محذوف

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some jurists say that a person customarily allowed to enter does not need to seek permission anew.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم إن من قد جرت العادة له بإباحة الدخول فهو غير محتاج إلى الاستئذان

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī rules that if a person peeping into someone’s home has his eye put out, the eye is forfeit and no compensation is due.
rows.anchor: قال الشافعي رحمه الله : لو فقئت عينه فهي هدر

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl ibn Saʿd reports that a man peered into the Prophet’s chamber with a small comb; the Prophet said he would have stabbed the man’s eye and stressed that permission precedes looking.
rows.anchor: تمسك بما روى سهل بن سعد قال : ( اطلع رجل في حجرة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that if a household gouges out the eye of someone peeking without permission, the eye is forfeit.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الرازي
rows.claim: Abū Bakr al-Rāzī rejects the report as contrary to legal analogy and consensus: if an unauthorized entrant’s eye is put out, the owner is liable to retaliation if intentional or compensation if accidental.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الرازي : هذا الخبر يرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī offers a possible construction of the report: a peeper looks at women’s private parts, persists after being stopped, and loses his eye during the ensuing resistance.
rows.anchor: فإن صح فمعناه : من اطلع في دار قوم ونظر إلى حرمهم ونسائهم فمونع فلم يمتنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Rāzī, a mere look followed by gouging without prior warning or resistance is an injury for which the perpetrator is liable, under 5:45.
rows.anchor: فأما إذا لم يكن إلا النظر ولم يقع فيه ممانعة ولا نهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the appeal to 5:45 begs the question: the verse applies when the eye is not already forfeited, which is exactly what the dispute must establish.
rows.anchor: لأنا أجمعنا على أن هذا النص مشروط بما إذا لم تكن العين مستحقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī distinguishes entering from peeping: visible entry lets residents know and cover themselves, while a hidden look can expose what they would not permit others to see, warranting stronger deterrence.
rows.anchor: لأنه إذا دخل علم القوم دخوله عليهم فاحترزوا عنه وتستروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī concludes that rejecting the Prophetic report on the basis of this argument is impermissible.
rows.anchor: وبالجملة فرد حديث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لهذا القدر من الكلام غير جائز
